nameStory: The name 'archangel' comes from the plant's hood-like flowers that resemble the protective wings of celestial beings. The 'yellow' part is obvious once you see it - this is the only member of the deadnettle family with bright golden-yellow blooms. Some folks call it 'golden dead-nettle' for the same reason, though it doesn't actually sting like true nettles.
description: Yellow archangel is a low-growing perennial plant in the mint family that spreads along the ground with creeping stems. It forms dense carpets about 6-12 inches tall in shaded areas, with heart-shaped leaves that often have silvery markings. The distinctive bright yellow flowers appear in clusters along square stems, making it unmistakable among New England's native plants. Originally from Europe, it has become established in many wooded areas as an escaped garden plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow hooded flowers in small clusters along the stem, each flower shaped like a tiny snapdragon with a lower lip for landing. The flowers have a subtle, sweet fragrance and feel papery when touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, often decorated with silvery-white patches or streaks. Leaves feel soft and slightly fuzzy, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading mats by sending out runners that root at the joints, creating dense colonies. Plants stay low to the ground but can cover large areas once established.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that are characteristic of the mint family - you can feel the four distinct corners when you roll the stem between your fingers. Stems are often purplish where they meet the leaf stalks.

habitat: Yellow archangel thrives in moist, shaded areas like deciduous and mixed forests, woodland edges, and shady garden spots. It prefers rich, well-drained soil and can tolerate various soil types as long as moisture is adequate. You'll often find it forming colonies under trees where few other plants can compete in the low light conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh, bright green leaves often showing prominent silver markings. Flowering begins in late spring, typically May, when the golden blooms are most abundant.
seasonality.summer: Flowering continues into early summer, though less profusely than in spring. The silvery leaf markings are most pronounced during the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Plants remain green well into fall, with leaves persisting longer than many other woodland plants. Some scattered blooming may continue in mild weather.
seasonality.winter: In protected areas, some leaves may persist through winter, appearing darker green and less silvery. The spreading stems remain visible, showing where new growth will emerge in spring.

funFact: Yellow archangel is sometimes called the 'aluminum plant' because its silvery leaf markings can be so metallic-looking that they actually reflect light like tiny mirrors, helping the plant capture more light in deep shade.
confusionNotes: The bright yellow flowers make this nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in the deadnettle family, which all have pink, purple, or white blooms. The heart-shaped, silver-marked leaves and spreading growth habit are also distinctive among woodland plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'dead-nettle,' this plant doesn't sting at all - the name comes from the resemblance of the leaves to stinging nettles, but without the sting (hence 'dead'). It's considered invasive in many areas because it can crowd out native woodland wildflowers, so some land managers work to control its spread.
compareHints: Yellow archangel stands out from its deadnettle relatives primarily by its golden flowers - red deadnettle has pink-purple blooms, henbit has smaller purple flowers, and white deadnettle has white flowers. It's also more of a woodland spreader compared to the other deadnettles, which are typically weedy annuals found in disturbed soils and gardens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red deadnettle differs from other Lamium species by its stalked, triangular-heart-shaped leaves and consistent purple-pink flower color.
Among the deadnettles, henbit is unique for its stem-clasping upper leaves - red deadnettle has all stalked leaves, while white and spotted deadnettles are much larger perennial plants.
Among its deadnettle relatives, spotted deadnettle is the only one with distinctive silvery-white leaf markings - red deadnettle and henbit have plain green leaves.
Among the deadnettles, cutleaf deadnettle stands out for its dramatically dissected leaves - much more deeply cut than red deadnettle's heart-shaped leaves or henbit's rounded, scalloped ones.
White deadnettle stands out from its relatives by its pure white flowers and perennial growth habit.
